title: Stare at one spot long enough and the things beside it really do vanish
hook: First noted by a Swiss doctor in 1804, it hides why our eyes keep jittering

open.title: Stare at the cross and the pink dots vanish
open.line: Pink dots sit in a ring on a gray background. Keep your eyes on the center cross and within seconds the dots get wiped away.

summary: Troxler fading, where still things around a fixed gaze vanish, was first recorded in 1804. Fixed eyes still make tiny jumps. Tests found they dropped just before things faded and rose just before they returned.

text: Stare only at the black cross,
and in seconds the pink dots fade one by one.
Stare a few seconds and the blotches seem to vanish.
In 1804, Swiss doctor Ignaz Troxler first noted it in Vienna.
Actually, it's explained by neural adaptation.
Visual nerves tune out unchanging input fast.
Even fixed on one spot, eyes keep making tiny jumps.
In 2006, Arizona researchers tracked 8 people's eyes
and had them press a button when a side target vanished.
Just before it vanished, microsaccades got fewer and smaller.
Just before it returned, they got more and bigger.
Early 1950s labs locked an image on one retinal spot as the eye moved.
The whole scene soon faded to one flat color.

sources: Martinez-Conde et al. (2006), Microsaccades Counteract Visual Fading during Fixation, Neuron 49
Troncoso et al. (2008), Microsaccades counteract perceptual filling-in, Journal of Vision
